newsitem.title: USA: Fans swarm New York procession for slain rapper.
newsitem.headline: Fans swarm New York procession for slain rapper.

text.p: More than 1,000 fans mobbed a motorcade carrying the body of rap superstar Notorious B.I.G. on Tuesday, causing pandemonium in the impoverished New York City neighbourhood where the slain musician once lived.

The motorcade followed funeral services in Manhattan for the rapper, 24, whose real name was Christopher Wallace. The heavyset Wallace, also known as Biggie Smalls, was killed in a drive-by shooting outside a Los Angeles party on March 9.

The procession bearing his body was led by four flower-filled cars, one with the letters B.I.G. spelled out in red carnations, through the Fort Greene and Bedford-Stuyvesant neighbourhoods of Brooklyn, where Wallace grew up and was a drug dealer before finding success in the music industry. More than a dozen limousines followed the hearse.
Fans yelled, screamed, applauded and cheered as the motorcade passed. Many chanted "B-I-G, B-I-G forever," and vendors hawked t-shirts bearing the rapper's likeness.

Police clad in riot gear and helmets tried to keep order, and some sprayed mace at the crowd. Four police officers and two civilians were hospitalized for skin burns and irritations from the repellant spray. Another civilian was treated at the scene.
A half-dozen people were arrested, including a reporter, on disorderly conduct and other misdemeanor charges.
Assistant Police Chief Joseph Dunne estimated the crowd at between 1,000 and 1,500 people. "The police acted responsibly and with a minimum of force," he added.
Traffic was stopped for blocks. Shopkeepers along the procession route pulled down their metal shutters to protect their stores from the unruly crowd.

Wallace's funeral in Manhattan was closed to the public, but those inside said several people, including producer Sean "Puffy" Combs, delivered remembrances of the star. Combs runs Wallace's record label, Bad Boy Entertainment, and was with him the night he was killed.

Also among the music industry celebrities at the funeral were a visibly emotional Queen Latifah; rappers Havoc of Mobb Deep, Nas and Busta Rhymes; and Run of Run-DMC, a pioneering rap trio, who goes by Rev. Run and preaches at a local church.

Others included Mary J. Blige, a popular hip-hop singer; members of the R&B quartet 112, whose debut hit single "Only You" featured an appearance by Wallace; and Lil' Kim, a female rapper and one of Wallace's proteges.

Also there were Flavor Flav of the influential rap group Public Enemy; SWV, a popular R&B female trio; Pepa of Salt-n-Pepa; Treach of Naughty By Nature; and M.C. Hammer, one of the first rap artists to attract a mainstream audience.
Former mayor David Dinkins, New York City's first black mayor, went to the funeral at the request of the family.
The Wallace killing remains unsolved. His bitter rival, Tupac Shakur, was killed in a similar ambush last year in Las Vegas. That slaying also is unsolved.

The two feuded in what was touted as a rivalry between West and East Coast rap, with Shakur's Los Angeles-based Death Row Records label run by Marion "Suge" Knight set against Wallace's and Combs' New York-based Bad Boy Entertainment.

Their public troubles began when Shakur was shot and robbed in 1994 in New York City, and he blamed Wallace and Combs. Shakur also boasted of having an affair with Wallace's estranged wife, Faith Evans, a popular R&B singer.
Many of the rappers and hip-hop artists at Wallace's funeral appeared on the Bad Boy label.

Wallace's 1994 debut album "Ready to Die" sold more than a million copies, and he was named rap artist of the year at the Billboard Awards in 1995. His album "Life After Death" is due to be released this month.
